post.caption: A red rose helped pay the rent. Hatton Garden, the London street of jewelers, is named for Sir Christopher Hatton, a favorite of Queen Elizabeth I who first impressed her with his dancing. In the 1570s, she had Ely's bishop lease him a garden, and the yearly rent included one red rose. The bishop's garden was famous for strawberries, and Shakespeare mentions them in Richard the Third. The jewelry trade arrived in the early 1800s, and after South African diamonds were found, the street became a world diamond market. Today it has nearly 300 jewelry businesses, and more than 70 of them are shops.
